h.strategy: Borrow interaction patterns from other empirical sciences: epistasis in genetics (the effect of one mutation depends on genetic background, and beneficial mutations help fitter backgrounds less), diminishing returns in economics, and redundancy in engineered systems. Translate each pattern into a concrete conditional hypothesis about how an edit's effect varies with the parent configuration. Favor predictions that a practitioner thinking only mechanistically would get wrong, especially background-dependent sign changes and weaker gains in already-strong parents. Use conditions that many parents satisfy. In the flaw step, discard analogies that do not transfer and keep only those with a plausible general reason to hold.

hyps.why: A strong direct 0->3 conv path gives diminishing returns for adding another 3x3 conv on the output edge.
Two parallel identity shortcuts into node 3 are redundant, so the second adds little or hurts.
Filling a missing direct 0->3 path with a conv gains much more than replacing an existing op.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 has no input and edge 4 is dead, so the edit has no benefit.
Removing the 0->2 branch when the direct 0->3 path is gone leaves fragile single-path connectivity.
Replacing a missing input edge with a conv restores the node 1 path and gives a large gain.
Pooling becomes the only processing on the node 2 path when its alternative branch is removed, so it hurts more.
With a strong direct conv path already present, an additional conv on 0->2 saturates and adds less.
A conv path via node 1 supplies capacity, so a gradient-friendly shortcut on 0->3 is complementary and gains more.
Replacing a strong conv on the chain with identity loses depth, which costs more than replacing a weak op.
